newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: Bearish bourse gives Lithuania dealers the blues.
newsitem.headline: Bearish bourse gives Lithuania dealers the blues.

text.p: Lithuania's bearish bourse, where some 500 companies are listed but only a fraction trade actively, has most local dealers singing the blues although they remain upbeat about the struggling market's prospects.
Shares on the Lithuanian bourse, launched as early as 1993 as one of the key adornments of a newly emergeny market, have been sliding steadily since a bull-run in January.
The gains in the first month of the year briefly raised hopes that Lithuania would emerge as a star performer in eastern Europe, but the bull-run soon fizzled out.

Local dealers hope that bargain prices, far cheaper than those on the star Baltic market Estonia, and the planned privatisation of key state assets will lure big-league foreign players to the bourse this year and also tempt locals.
The market currently has a market capitalisation of 5.6 billion litas ($1.4 billion).
A brief survey of five Lithuanian brokerage houses conducted by Reuters found dealers divided over when they think prices and activity will pick up and the general mood was gloomy.
The most optimistic forecast saw prices rising slowly next week while the most cautious saw prices up at the end of summer.
One dealer was unsure and two saw slight gains in two to four weeks time.
However, there was a consensus that things will start rolling by autumn at the latest with hopes that serious portfolio investors will come to the market.
"Serious investors are only examining the market now... it won't pick up before summer," said Kestutis Kupsys of brokerage firm Mendes Prior Europe.
His comments were echoed by others, who said long-term investors were expected to arrive in the next few months.
A group of senior fund managers visited Lithuania last week on a fact finding-mission.
Members of the delegation said Lithuania's equities market had a lot of potential for future growth and lucrative returns.
In the January bull-run, the Litin A index, which tracks the bourse's most active listings, surged to 3,242.25, over double its late October value.
Things have been mostly downhill ever since, with the index tumbling 158.89 points on Thursday to 2,219.55.
On the bright side, the index is still over a third higher than its October level.

Dealers said January's rapid climb had been fuelled by domestic buyers and was for the most speculative. The gains were also touched off by a switch to equities from debt in response to falling Treasury bill yields.
"January's situation was not based on any careful examination of companies," said one dealer.
"Today's situation has not been helped by disappointing first quarter results," he added.
The government's commitment to selling off attractive state enterprises, a good macroeconomic climate and political stability bode well for the future, they said.
But in the short-term, local dealers see no reason to change their gloomy tune.
Brokerage house Suprema is the exception to the rule, although its dealers are far from bullish about the short-term.
"Prices may begin rising slightly next week simply because they are so low now," said Arvydas Jacikevicius of Suprema.
-- Riga newsroom, +371 721 52 40 ($ = 3.998 Lithuanian Litas)
